The text area grows to 420 px and then scrolls under a toolbar that stays.", "opts": { "label": "Article", "value": "

A small search index, built by hand

\n

Most teams reach for a hosted search service the moment a list grows past a few hundred rows. This note walks through the opposite choice: an inverted index kept in memory, rebuilt in under a second, and small enough to read in one sitting.

\n

What the index holds

\n

For every word, the index keeps the list of documents that contain it, with the positions. A query becomes a handful of list intersections, which is fast as long as the lists stay sorted.

\n
  • A tokenize() step that lowercases and splits on word boundaries
  • A posting list per term, sorted by document id
    • positions inside the document, for phrase queries
    • a term frequency, for ranking
  • A small table of document lengths
\n

Measure before you optimise. The first version of the index was a plain object of arrays, and it was fast enough for eighteen months.

\n

Building it

\n
  1. Read every document once.
  2. Split it into terms and drop the stop words.
  3. Append the document id to each term's list.
  4. Sort the lists, then freeze the whole structure.
\n
function build(docs) {\n  const index = new Map();\n  for (const doc of docs) {\n    for (const [pos, term] of tokenize(doc.text).entries()) {\n      if (!index.has(term)) index.set(term, []);\n      index.get(term).push([doc.id, pos]);\n    }\n  }\n  return index;\n}
\n

The loop above is the whole build. Everything else is bookkeeping: a custom hash table a Map was plenty, and the sort happens once at the end.

\n
\n

Ranking, briefly

\n

A document scores higher when the query terms are rare across the collection and frequent inside it. The classic formula is term frequency times inverse document frequency; a small length correction keeps long documents from winning by bulk.

\n

Further reading lives on the ranking notes page, and questions go to index-team@example.org.

\n

Where it stops being enough

\n

Past a few hundred thousand documents the rebuild takes long enough to notice, and memory becomes the limit. That is the point to persist the posting lists and load them lazily, not before.
